title: Mahajanaka's swim
hook: shipwrecked, he swims seven days without seeing land, because effort is never wasted

segments.voice: Yesterday, Temiya the silent prince, sixteen years without a word. Your line was silence can be a choice. Did you find your ten quiet minutes? Day ninety-five.

A thesis in its third draft. A recovery that moves an inch a week. A job hunt on its fortieth application. Some projects have no shore in sight. And at some point a reasonable voice asks: what's the point? You can't even see the end. Today's story is the second of the ten long Jatakas, and it's that question, asked in the middle of the ocean. A prince, a sinking ship, and a goddess who wants to know why he's still swimming.
screen: `A PROJECT WITH NO SHORE IN SIGHT.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: Mahajanaka is a prince born in exile. His father, the king of Mithila, was killed by his own brother, and his mother fled while pregnant. When the boy grows up and learns the truth, he decides to win back what was lost. So he joins a trading ship bound for a far country to make his fortune. Out at sea, the ship breaks apart. The others weep and pray and drown. Mahajanaka, the story says, does something practical. He eats his fill, soaks his clothes in oil against the cold water, climbs the mast, and leaps as far out as he can, clear of the wreck and the sea creatures. Then he swims. And he keeps swimming. Seven days, the story says, with no land in sight. On the seventh day, a sea goddess named Manimekhala appears above the waves and asks him, in effect: why are you bothering? There's no shore. You'll die out here. His answer is the heart of the story. He says a person who makes the effort, even if they die trying, is free from blame, and that giving up guarantees failure while effort at least gives a chance. Effort is never wasted. Moved by his answer, she lifts him out of the sea and carries him to Mithila, where, in time, he becomes king. In the tradition, this life shows the perfection of viriya: effort, energy, courage that keeps going. Not effort because success is certain. Effort because it's the only part that's yours.
screen: `A PRINCE BORN IN EXILE.` · `THE SHIP BREAKS APART.` · `SEVEN DAYS, NO LAND IN SIGHT.` · `THE GODDESS ASKS: WHY BOTHER?` · then, large: `SWIM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing find its rhythm, like a steady stroke. Bring to mind one thing you're working on where you can't see the end. Hold it gently. Notice the tiredness that comes with it, and the voice that asks why bother. Then, with each out-breath, picture one stroke. Not the shore. Just this stroke, then the next. When your mind drifts, that's fine: you come back, which is its own kind of stroke. The bell holds the time.
Mahajanaka's swim. Seven days in the open sea, because effort is never wasted.
Your line: swim anyway. Today, give ten honest minutes to the thing with no shore in sight. One stroke. Day ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 95 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 2 CLOSE: THE WHOLE LIFE.`

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Mahajanaka story as an example of viriya, effort, and in Theravada countries such as Thailand it is retold in books, art and temple murals.

match.prompt: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

the sea goddess who asked why

myth: Mahajanaka swam because he could see the shore
for seven days there was no land in sight. he swam anyway.
he ate, oiled his clothes, climbed the mast, and leapt clear of the wreck.
the goddess rescued him because he prayed to her
she was moved by his answer: effort is never wasted.

fork.setup: you've swum for seven days. a goddess appears and says there's no shore: why bother? what do you say?
options: effort is never wasted, even if I die trying.
fork.reveal: he defends his effort, and she's so moved that she carries him to Mithila, where he later becomes king.

original.note: Pali: effort, energy; the perfection the tradition links with Mahajanaka's life.

trapdoor: what you thought: a survival story at sea.
what it means: the perfection of effort, which keeps going because the effort is the part that's yours.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 539 is the second of the ten great births, and later in the same story he renounces the throne after seeing a fruiting mango tree stripped bare.

notes: Plot details (the uncle killing the king, the preparations before the leap, seven days, Manimekhala's question and his answer) are paraphrased from Jataka 539; confirm.
The trapdoor mentions the later mango-tree episode; confirm, and that it isn't taught today.
The viriya / vira link is a common etymological gloss; confirm.
Thailand: King Bhumibol's retelling made the story widely taught; left unnamed in the voice.
